item.title: Nations Blast Fossil Fuel Sector’s Sway on UN Climate Deal
item.description: Global climate talks entered their final hours with nations in Europe, Central America and the Pacific criticizing a proposed agreement’s failure to address fossil fuels and accusing the oil and gas sector of swaying negotiations in the industry’s favor.
item.dc:creator: list.metadata.agency
item.content:encoded: (Bloomberg) -- Global climate talks entered their final hours with nations in Europe, Central America and the Pacific criticizing a proposed agreement’s failure to address fossil fuels and accusing the oil and gas sector of swaying negotiations in the industry’s favor.A draft deal presented to delegates from almost 200 countries omitted any reference to fossil fuels, the largest contributor to global warming, and pledged support for carbon-capture technology, a climate tool favored by energy producers. “There are some who don’t want us to use the word ‘fossil fuels’ at this COP,” German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider told a meeting Friday at the United Nations COP31 summit in Antalya, Turkey. “There are some who make a lot of money with that.”The European Union has concerns that the draft text published Thursday casts the two-week-long meeting as a fossil-fuel COP, and sees a risk of talks ending without any agreed deal if there aren’t substantial changes, said a senior official for the bloc, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss private deliberations.COP31 President Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, along with other officials, insists the text doesn’t require a specific acknowledgement on transitioning away from fossil fuels — since nations committed to that at the 2023 talks held in Dubai and the pledge still stands.Envoys and government officials, including Saudi Arabia’s Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, were continuing to wrangle over the summit’s potential outcomes Friday, with discussions expected to continue into the weekend.But there were deep divisions over key elements of the talks, and negotiating nations’ positions were hardening, potentially diminishing the odds of the conference ending with a broad, ambitious declaration. “Everything seems pretty stuck,” said Ilana Seid, Palau’s representative to the UN and the chair of the Alliance of Small Island States. “There are a lot of positions that cut into other coalition red lines, and there seems to be very little room for movement.” Negotiators meeting in Antalya are under pressure to deliver a more decisive response on global warming with greenhouse gas emissions still rising, and as political and corporate appetite for climate action wanes in nations, including the US. A year of deadly extreme weather disasters has underscored the risks of a hotter planet, and a recent UN assessment concluded the world can no longer limit the increase in global temperatures to 1.5C, a key target of the 2015 Paris Agreement.For imperiled Pacific Island nations, a global move away from fossil fuels “is not a political choice,” Jess Gasper, environment minister for the Marshall Islands, told the summit Friday. “It is a matter of survival.”In one of the summit’s most forthright attacks on the oil and gas sector, Panama’s environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro on Wednesday accused COP31 of being held hostage by a “petroleum mafia.” In a letter sent to the event’s presidency, Panama outlined an array of demands, including a cap on global oil production, and threatened to withhold support for a final deal. “This is a climate change COP,” Navarro told reporters Friday, referring to the talks that are formally known as the Conference of the Parties. “We won’t let it become the Conference of Petroleum.”The latest draft proposed greater deployment of carbon-capture technology and included a potential target to capture at least 500 million tons of carbon dioxide by 2035, while working toward a goal of 2.5 gigatons. Currently fewer than 0.2% of fossil-fuel emissions are captured, according to the Global Carbon Budget.Negotiators have been told that removing the carbon-capture language isn’t an option — but neither is incorporating a transition away from fossil fuels — Seid told Bloomberg. The small island states coalition is exploring “creative” options to resolve the impasses and is looking for a more “balanced” approach, she said.Australia’s climate change and energy minister, Chris Bowen, who is leading COP31 negotiations, acknowledged the carbon-capture language isn’t many people’s first choice.“We’ll continue to talk to parties about what’s necessary to best reflect a consensus view,” Bowen told reporters. Delegates from Panama, France and other countries on Friday laid down six demands, including ensuring science is the foundation for all outcomes, clear language on transitioning away from fossil fuels and fair finance contributions. The small island state alliance said it needs to see stronger language on the tripling of adaptation finance and wants an embrace of the “best available science” provided by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.The draft agreement circulated Thursday did lay out potential compromises on issues including climate finance, trade curbs and the timing of some key science reports. The document also included a pledge to boost electricity’s share of global final energy demand to 35% by 2035, from just over 20% currently. Summit organizers have rallied more than 60 countries behind a voluntary pledge and are seeking to include the goal in the final COP31 declaration, putting it on a more formal footing.--With assistance from Lili Pike.(Updates with new details on negotiating positions from seventh paragraph.)More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: NYC Fitness Buffs Bristle at City Plan to Close Outdoor Gym
item.description: In New York’s neighborhood-level disputes over government projects, even pull-up bars have become a flashpoint.
item.dc:creator: list.metadata.agency
item.content:encoded: (Bloomberg) -- In New York’s neighborhood-level disputes over government projects, even pull-up bars have become a flashpoint.At Tompkins Square Park in Manhattan, the paint on a set of bars is chipping. But the fitness buffs who work out in the park daily are holding on to them for dear life. At issue are city proposals to close the outdoor gym for months and replace it with equipment that is more accessible to people with disabilities.Regulars argue the equipment is sufficiently accessible and that the city could reconstruct it with inferior materials. Some simply dread a monthslong separation from the bars that have become part of their daily lives.For Theophilus London, the stakes feel particularly personal. About three months ago, when he was struggling and looking to change his life, he found his way to the pull-up bars in Tompkins Square Park.“I was in a desperate need of a change of lifestyle,” London said on a recent afternoon, between sets at the East Village park. “This park changed my life.”London, a musician nominated for a Grammy Award with Kanye West in 2016, visits the pull-up bars daily. He is among many park-goers speaking against plans to close the decades-old fitness equipment for renovations.The park adds to a list of government projects that some New Yorkers have perceived as community interference.A few blocks southwest, in Nolita, residents protested the construction of an affordable housing project at Elizabeth Street Garden for more than a decade. Across the East River in Brooklyn, plans to build a skate park at Mount Prospect Park concerned neighborhood groups that said the facility would exacerbate the problem of higher temperatures in urban areas.“The idea that it’s an adult fitness area that needs reconstruction is totally and completely misguided,” said Salo Coslovsky, an urban planning professor at New York University, at a recent local advisory board meeting on the Tompkins Square Park pull-up bars. Coslovsky questioned the expertise of consultants working on the project. “I don’t know if they actually do pull-ups and push-ups and dips,” he said, adding that thousands who signed an online petition opposing the renovations disagreed with the consultants’ assessment. It now has roughly 3,700 signatures.The park’s alterations would reconstruct the basketball courts and double the size of the park’s pool. The project received $6.1 million from New York Governor Kathy Hochul through an initiative to improve public swimming facilities, and another $2.8 million from Mayor Zohran Mamdani, according to city records.Department of Parks and Recreation Commissioner Tricia Shimamura said in a statement that she was committed to making parks accessible and that her department has worked to reduce the amount of time the exercise equipment would be closed. The city is collecting input from residents, including by sending park designers to meetings of the neighborhood advisory board. The meetings have run long to accommodate public comment from people who say shutting down the bars would be a grave mistake.Jahmal Kirwan is part of a larger group with London that works out at the bars. A lifelong resident of Lower Manhattan, Kirwan said he’s not against improving the park.About two years ago, he said, the bars and the community around them helped him recover from the “brink of death,” when he was drinking and partying every day. He worries the city could delay the renovations, like other nearby developments, leaving a community without a meeting place for too long as it awaits a finished product. Kirwan said he’d gone his whole life without attending a local advisory board meeting, until he learned about the looming closure of the pull-up bars. He’s attended over the past few months to voice his concerns.“It’s like them closing down the rehab,” Kirwan said. In regard to a city proposal to close the bars for about 18 months, he said, “there are going to be people that never get to see the bars, because they might not even survive.”More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: From Aramco to Saudi’s $1.2 trillion wealth fund HQ: Why Houthis are targeting kingdom’s economic nerve centres
item.description: Houthi attacks on Saudi Aramco and the $1 trillion Public Investment Fund headquarters in Riyadh are raising concerns over the security of the kingdom’s economic nerve centres, threatening Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030 ambitions and investor confidence.
item.dc:creator: Bhanu Pratap
item.content:encoded: Saudi Arabia’s economic ambitions are increasingly coming under attack as Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels expand their strikes beyond oil infrastructure to some of the kingdom’s most prominent financial landmarks. The latest target is the headquarters of the Public Investment Fund (PIF), the sovereign wealth fund central to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s plan to transform the Saudi economy. The 80-storey PIF Tower in Riyadh’s King Abdullah Financial District was struck on Thursday, damaging several floors of the building. Windows across seven to eight floors were blown out, while parts of its metal facade were left bent, according to a Reuters journalist who visited the site. Repair crews were reportedly seen replacing damaged glass shortly after the attack. Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence confirmed that a tower in the capital’s financial district had been targeted in what it described as a terrorist attack by the Houthis. The strike caused material damage to the building and nearby structures, but no casualties were reported, the state news agency SPA said. An accompanying photograph released by the authorities showed damage to the PIF headquarters. The attack marks the second time in less than two weeks that the Houthis have struck a major landmark associated with Saudi Arabia’s economic ambitions. On November 8, the group targeted the Riyadh headquarters of state-owned oil giant Saudi Aramco, another symbol of the kingdom’s economic power. The latest strikes raise questions about the security of Saudi Arabia’s financial and commercial infrastructure at a time when Riyadh is seeking to attract international investors, diversify its economy and establish itself as a global business hub. Why are the Houthis targeting Saudi Arabia’s economic nerve centres? The choice of targets carries significance beyond the physical damage inflicted. Saudi Aramco represents the kingdom’s oil wealth, while the PIF is the financial engine behind its ambitious economic diversification programme. With assets of around $1 trillion, the sovereign wealth fund finances and invests in projects spanning tourism, infrastructure, technology, entertainment and sports. It is central to Vision 2030, Mohammed bin Salman’s flagship programme to reduce the kingdom’s dependence on oil revenues and create alternative sources of economic growth.The King Abdullah Financial District, where the PIF Tower is located, is also a major part of Riyadh’s ambition to become an international financial centre. Striking these landmarks therefore carries a wider economic and psychological message: even the institutions underpinning Saudi Arabia’s long-term transformation plans are within the Houthis’ reach. The Houthis claimed to have targeted Riyadh’s financial centre twice on Thursday, once at dawn and again in the evening. The group also announced attacks on King Khalid International Airport, Khamis Mushait airbase in southern Saudi Arabia and the SADAF Petrochemical Company in Jubail. Saudi authorities had not immediately confirmed these additional claims. The Saudi-led coalition said it had dealt with a missile threat launched towards Riyadh, with debris falling in the area. The kingdom’s foreign ministry said it reserved the right to take all necessary measures to defend its sovereignty and protect its citizens and national assets. Saudi Arabia faces a prolonged conflict The escalation comes as Saudi Arabia confronts the prospect of a prolonged military campaign in Yemen. According to Reuters, Saudi officials now anticipate that the conflict could stretch for another six months, citing sources familiar with the kingdom’s plans. Riyadh reportedly wants its allies on the ground to make territorial gains before entering negotiations with the Houthis. The Saudi-led coalition has also replaced its commander overseeing operations in Yemen. The conflict has become increasingly complicated for Riyadh. The Houthis have expanded their control over strategically important parts of Yemen, including the country's Red Sea coastline and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical shipping route connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. The group has also made gains around Taiz, while forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government have faced setbacks. Saudi Arabia first intervened in Yemen in 2015, leading an Arab coalition after the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and large parts of the country. The intervention failed to produce a decisive victory, and a ceasefire reached in 2022 largely held until hostilities reignited this year.The renewed conflict is now threatening to undermine the kingdom’s economic priorities. Repeated attacks on oil facilities, airports and financial infrastructure could complicate efforts to reassure foreign investors about the security and stability of the country.With inputs from Reuters.
